1:
Keil sets the scale of the piece before touching a word of it: the song covers the whole future history of Israel and carries the marks of prophetic testimony, drawing an ideal picture of the benefits the Lord conferred and of the ingratitude that repaid them; he quotes a description of it as soaring to the loftiest heights, concise and pictorial in style, rough and penetrating yet full of the holiest solemnity, at once a witness against a disobedient nation and a miniature of the whole life of the man who spoke it.

The appeal to heaven and earth is explained the same way by two and differently by a third. Henry takes it as an appeal to the truth of what follows and the justice of God's proceedings, and gives the reason that these would sooner hear than a perverse people, since they have never revolted from obedience to their Creator and will therefore rise up in judgment. Wesley says the lifeless creatures are called partly to accuse the stupidity of a people duller of hearing than they, and partly as witnesses. Calvin looks at the effect on the hearers: the magnificent opening is there lest they disdain the song in their pride or reject it outright, since the world will endure no strain that does not tickle the ear with praise, while this one stigmatises their perverse nature, obstinate ingratitude and incorrigible contumacy, and was meant to echo daily from their own tongues, which made it more offensive still. Ellicott notes that the opening is almost identical with a prophet's, save that the two words for hearing change places.

Whether the second verse is a wish or a promise is contested. Gill reports the reading that makes it a prayer that the words might fall like rain and penetrate men's hearts, and prefers a prophecy of what would be; and he sets the doctrine here against the law, fiery where this is cooling, a storm where this is a gentle rain, terrible where this is desirable. Calvin names those who resolve the future tense into the optative and thinks them wrong, since the speaker celebrates the fruitfulness the Spirit actually imparts rather than asking for it, and such a request would have been unseasonable; the comparison means that if the people were soil in a state of softness the doctrine would irrigate them to abundant fruitfulness. Keil finds the point of comparison in the refreshing and fertilising power of dew and rain, Wesley in the softening of hearts.

The words are then weighed. Clarke derives the noun from a root meaning to gain over the heart by persuasive speech, notes that the Greek version renders it by a term for a weighty sententious saying, and reads the figure progressively, the rain beginning slowly and increasing until the whole canon of revelation is complete. Ellicott renders it rather as learning, that which is received, and builds a chain on it, everything from the Father of lights being handed from one heavenly messenger to another until it reaches a man in the form he can best receive. On the next clause Gill and Keil agree against a common rendering: the verb is to proclaim the name, not call upon it. Calvin points out that the clause stands last though it gives the reason for what precedes, since unless the hearers submit reverently God is defrauded of his honour; Wesley glosses the name as the excellencies and righteous actions by which God has made himself known. Henry stops at the title that follows and observes that this is the first place in Scripture where God is called a Rock, a figure for power and faithfulness that cannot be moved, and for the shelter those countries found against sun and tempest.
4:
The title that opens the song is contested at the root. Clarke reports that eminent critics render the word Creator, that one ancient version reads it so, and that a great Jewish authority held it to mean origin, fountain, first cause, so that the line should run that he is the first principle and his work is perfect. He allows that the usual rendering gives a very good sense, rocks being in those lands the ordinary places of defence. The others build on that rendering without hesitation. Gill notes that the word stands first for emphasis and is written with an enlarged letter to mark the greatness of the person meant, identifying it with the rock struck in the wilderness. Ellicott makes the name a characteristic of the whole song, traces it to the smiting of the rock at Horeb, and observes that the confession was carried in the very names of Israel's leaders, one meaning that God is a rock, another that the bearer was redeemed by the rock. Wesley takes the figure for stability of nature and invincible power and for fixedness in counsel, so that any sad change in a man's affairs proceeds from himself and not from God.

What the string of attributes is doing is answered by two. Ellicott says no such combination of all the words for uprightness, sincerity, equity and reliability occurs anywhere else in Scripture. Calvin warns against taking the expressions generally, which obscures their meaning and lessens their force: the perfection of God's works stands deliberately against the rebellion of the people, since if anything in them were defective or his truth doubtful, there would have been some natural excuse.

The verse that follows is the hardest in the song, and all say so. Ellicott reports that many interpreters give the first two lines up as hopeless, not because the words are hard to translate but because of the number of possible interpretations, and offers his own after consulting a learned Hebrew. Clarke sets out two conjectural renderings, one following the Samaritan text, and then turns on the interpretation commonly given, that God's children have their spots but sin in them is not as sin in others and that God does not see their sins as he sees those of his enemies. He calls the doctrine bad and denies that the text gives it any foundation. Wesley arrives at the same place by a shorter road, taking the stain as proof that these are not God's children at all, and adding that the text does not affirm they have any spot whatever. Keil explains the construction rather than the doctrine, treating the clause as parenthetical apposition, taking the word in the moral sense of a stain, and observing that had it stood after the subject, no difficulty would have arisen.

The reproach is read as an argument from benefits received. Calvin says the recital of God's bounty begins here to expose the ingratitude to greater infamy, since the more liberally God deals with us the more earnest our piety ought to be; he doubts not that the hearers would have raged had they not known the speaker was already called to die. Keil takes the verse as the theme's expansion, the perversity showing in repaying with apostasy the God to whom the nation owed its existence. Ellicott notes that the first line is an exclamatory question, that question and exclamation bear one name among the rabbinical writers, and that the verb rendered bought is the word used at the birth of Cain. Wesley presses the three verbs in turn, bought as redeemed from bondage, made not merely by creation but by being formed into a peculiar people, established as favour renewed and not withdrawn; and he asks who has bewitched a people that would forsake their own mercies for lying vanities.
7:
What the days of old are is not agreed, and the disagreement follows from how each reads the song. Keil takes the summons as a call to reflect on what the Lord had done, and identifies the years of generation after generation with the deliverance out of Egypt, reaching back before Moses and forward a little past him. Henry reads it as an appeal to the records, bidding them remember the history of those days and the providences concerning the old world and the patriarchs, in which a constant series of mercies may be traced. Gill looks the other way, listing deliverances still future when the words were spoken, from the judges and the days of David down through the captivity to the age of the Maccabees, since he takes the song as addressed to a much later generation. Calvin makes the verse an explanation of the one before, and gives the motive: a people inflated by their present standing are reminded of their origin and told to consider not what they are but from what they were taken, since men who forget that all they have proceeded from God are blinded by their dignity and despise others. Ellicott notes only that the verse falls plainly into four parts.

The division of the nations draws the boldest reconstruction from Clarke, who reports on another's authority that these verses warrant believing the earth was divided very early by divine command and probably by lot; since one continent is elsewhere called the land of Ham it presumably fell to him, another to Japheth and another to Shem, with Palestine reserved as the Lord's portion for a people not yet in being. He calls the whole movement the general migration and has it commanded to Noah and passed on by him to his sons. Gill keeps to the same principle without the map, naming the generation in whose days the earth was divided and whose name records it, and pressing that men did not seize what they pleased but each had his parcel allotted by the Lord himself.

Wesley goes further. The lands were disposed so as to reserve room for the numbers Israel would become, and to that end the hearts of several peoples were so guided that the posterity of Canaan, already accursed, settled in the very country intended for Israel, so that when their iniquities were ripe they might be rooted out. Keil stays with the sentence, taking the boundaries to be fixed with reference to the number of the sons of Israel, so that from the forming of nations God had cared for this people.

The reason given for all this is where the strongest language falls. Calvin insists that nothing moved God but his own good pleasure, and that the words do not mean there was anything better in this people; they assign why one nation was preferred to the rest of mankind, that he took it to himself as his hereditary portion, a dignity depending wholly on gratuitous election. Keil says the same in his own terms, the choice being made before the nation existed, and explains the figure of the second clause as a measuring cord, then a piece of land measured off, and so applied to the people. Wesley reduces it to one sentence, that it is no wonder God had so great a regard to them when he had chosen them out of all mankind for his peculiar portion. Clarke alone turns it round and finds the astonishment in the exchange: as holy souls take God for their portion, so God takes them for his, representing himself as happy in his followers, while a man seeking an earthly portion has little commerce with the Most High. Gill extends the title to a spiritual Israel taken into covenant.
10:
The verb that opens the passage is weighed by two. Ellicott points out that the whole verse stands in the pictorial present in Hebrew, and that finding is a word common to both Testaments for God's first revealing of himself to a man, as when the angel found Hagar by the fountain. Wesley denies that any chance is meant, taking it of one looking out and seeking; he distinguishes the manifestation in Egypt from the eminent finding in the wilderness, and hears in the word both that they were lost in themselves and that their recovery came from elsewhere. Calvin observes what is left out: had the intention been to record every instance of God's kindness the recital must have begun from Abraham, as a psalmist's does from the original covenant.

The eagle divides them on a point of natural history. Clarke offers two accounts, that she flutters over the brood to excite them to fly, or, as some think, disturbs the nest to oblige the young to leave it; and he takes the second, so that God by his plagues obliged a reluctant people to leave a place he had marked for destruction. Gill reports a rabbinic account that runs the other way, the eagle being merciful to her young and not entering the nest suddenly but first making a noise and shaking it, that they may be fitter to receive her. Wesley presses the last clause, that the young are carried as on the wings and not in the claws, gently and safely and without fear of hurting them, and reports the belief that the eagle does usually so carry them. Keil keeps the figure whole, an eagle teaching its young to fly and shielding them with watchful affection.

The exclusive clause that follows is read as forestalling an excuse. Calvin says it is spoken by anticipation, to take away every pretext from a people accustomed to mingle superstitions with the pure service of God, whose standing plea when they imported the gods of every nation was that God was not thereby robbed of his own honour. Clarke states the fact more flatly, that help came from no other quarter and that the Egyptian gods could not save their own worshippers. Wesley draws the inference against the hearers, that they were the more unworthy for giving idols a share in worship owed to God alone.

On the description of the land Clarke makes a grammatical claim the others do not: all the verbs here stand in the future, so that this is prophecy of a prosperity still to come, in which even the rocky part of the country would be made fertile. Keil takes the driving over the high places as a figure for the victorious subjugation of a land, and Wesley says plainly that to ride upon, in the language of Scripture, is to subdue; he explains the honey by bees that made it in the holes of the rocks and the oil by olives that bear most in rocky ground. Gill reads the high places as towers and fortified cities, citing a paraphrase that has the people made to dwell in the towers of the land. Calvin dismisses as frivolous the notion that the country was so called for being the navel of the earth, weighs the usage by which men go down into Egypt and up into Judea, and inclines rather to take the term of its excellency. On the last verse the fat of the kidneys is explained alike by three: Clarke compares the germ of the grain to the kidney within its coat of purest fat, Ellicott notes that the metaphor is carried over literally from the Hebrew and that this was the fat the law reserved for the altar.
15:
The name at the head of the passage divides them. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all derive it from a word for upright, and each draws a reproach from the derivation: Gill that the people ought to have been such and professed to be, Wesley that the title both reminds them what they professed and shames them for degenerating from it, Clarke that a people once really walking in righteousness would in the time foretold not merely revolt but fight against God, like a full-fed horse that will not bear the harness but breaks away and kicks at his master. Ellicott takes the word differently, as a diminutive and a term of endearment, either the child of the upright or the beloved Israel, since the letters of the diminutive of Israel slightly abbreviated would yield it; he notes that it belongs to this book and one prophet only, that two Targums render it simply Israel while a third keeps the word, and that the Greek translates it the beloved one. Henry sorts the apostasy into two counts, the first being security and sensuality, pride and insolence and the common abuses of plenty. Calvin quotes the proverb that satiety breeds violence, but lays the blame on men's own depravity, who ought rather to be made humble by loving-kindness.

On the provoking to jealousy Calvin enters a caution and then presses the figure. Jealousy is ascribed to God only figuratively, since he is free from all passions; but because men never sufficiently reflect what pollution they contract by idolatry, the grossness of the sin has to be put in such terms, transferring his honour to another being no lighter an offence than a licentious woman wounding her husband by running after adulterers. Wesley glosses it the same way, jealousy being the rage of a man and the ground of the anger their falseness to a God accepted as husband. Gill dissents from the whole reading: he takes the word rendered strange gods to mean simply others, notes that the people were not idolaters after the return from Babylon, and refers it to the other saviours and messiahs set up after the rejection of Christ, none having been attempted before his coming. Keil says only that these verses expand the one before them.

The word rendered devils is surveyed by Clarke across the versions: the Syriac, Chaldee, Targums and Samaritan keep the original term, while the Latin, Greek, Arabic, Persic, Coptic and Anglo-Saxon give devils or demons, the Arabic using the plural of the name of Satan. Wesley explains the double statement, that these were idols brought into the world by devils in opposition to God, in which they manifested themselves and gave answers, while the Gentiles professed to worship God in them and were deluded with the pretence that these were a sort of lower gods. Ellicott notes that an apostle repeats the phrase, and renders the clause about new gods as those that came from close at hand, comparing the idol made out of firewood.

On the closing reproach Ellicott again unsettles the text. He offers as another possible rendering that the Rock has begotten thee forgetful and thou hast forgotten the God that travailed with thee, notes that the second expression occurs in a psalm ascribed to the same author, and observes of the word he renders forgetful that it is usually taken as a verb although no such verb occurs elsewhere, so that it has been invented for this passage. Clarke keeps to his earlier rendering of the title, the first cause and fountain of being. Gill reports a version making it the rock of thy kindred, a brother by incarnation; Wesley refers the title either to God or to the Christ whom the Israelites tempted. Calvin fixes the aggravation, that they did not fall through ignorance but wilfully stifled a knowledge which ought to have shone in every heart.
19:
What the seeing means is answered three ways. Keil takes it as no more than the causal link between apostasy and punishment. Clarke renders the line more literally, that the Lord saw and through indignation reprobated his sons and daughters, and paraphrases it as the moment of being justly incensed. Calvin makes it a statement about forbearance in judgment, that God does not act hastily or become alienated from his children without weighing their case, as elsewhere he goes down to see whether a city's cry is what it is reported to be; and he adds that God can need no such examination, since nothing escapes him. Henry sets the passage in its place, since the song follows the order of the predictions in the chapter before, so that the resolves of divine justice come immediately after the revolt; and he warns that we deceive ourselves if we think God will be mocked by a faithless people who play fast and loose with him. Wesley marks that they were sons and daughters by calling and profession, and Gill refers the verse to a later rejection.

The clause about faith is corrected the same way by two. Clarke renders it that there is no steadfastness in them and they can never be depended on, being fickle because faithless. Ellicott makes the point exactly: the word is not used in the sense of belief or confidence but as when we speak of keeping faith or breaking it, so that these are children with whom no faith will be kept. Wesley says the same in a phrase, that they are perfidious and have broken a covenant solemnly made; Keil renders the earlier half as a generation full of perversities.

The retaliation is read by everyone as the calling of the Gentiles. Clarke calls the verse a very pointed promise of that calling in consequence of the rejection, and notes that an apostle applies it to precisely that event. Ellicott reports the same application, adding that it proves Israel had been informed of the calling beforehand, and pairs it with a prophet's words about being found of them that sought him not. Calvin describes its shape: after withdrawing for a time God becomes the open enemy and repays in kind, so that as they set empty phantoms in antagonism with him, he exalts barbarous nations against them, the figure again drawn from jealous husbands. Wesley defines the no-people sharply, as nations without the knowledge and fear of God, which he calls the foundation of all true policy and government, and yet to be taken in Israel's stead. Gill alone keeps the first clause on home ground, referring the no-god to the false Christs that arose after the true one.

On the fire the difference is one of reach. Clarke takes the phrase for the deepest destruction and a total extermination, reads the foundations of the mountains as the strongest fortresses, and finds the whole fulfilled in the last Roman destruction of the city, where of the fortifications not one stone was left. Gill applies it the same way, to the burning of the city and temple. Ellicott stays with the words, noting that a prophet quotes the line and reporting a rabbinic gloss making the foundations of the mountains the city founded upon them. Calvin keeps it as metaphor while insisting that more is expressed here than in the many other places where the figure occurs, since this fire penetrates to the deepest abysses and spares not the very roots of the mountains. Wesley turns it into questions and then extends it past this world: are they proud of their plenty, it will burn up the increase of the earth; are they confident of their strength, it will destroy the foundations of the mountains; and the misery it brings them to here is only a faint resemblance of a misery without end.
24:
The scourges are counted differently. Clarke numbers them as arrows shot in succession, famine first, then burning heat which he takes either of a rainless sky or rather of boils and pestilential fevers, then the plague, then the multiplying of wild beasts, and last the poisonous serpents. Calvin reduces them to three, pestilence and famine and the sword, the standing triad on which the prophets constantly dilate, and explains why particulars are given at all: generalities would not have affected the hearers, so specimens are adduced to inspire greater terror. Gill supplies the local colour, a paraphrase rendering the first stroke as being swollen with famine, a word a historian used of the siege of the city, and a rabbinic reading that would make it the hairs of hunger, since a famishing man's hair grows. Wesley describes the same stroke as burning and parching the inward parts and blackening the face, and takes the heat of fevers or carbuncles.

On the next verse Keil divides the field exactly, the sword sweeping away the men outside in the slaughter itself while the defenceless perish in the chambers from alarm, the young man and the virgin, the suckling and the grey head; and he names a scholar who applied the second word to hunger and plague and says he is wrong, since it means a sudden mortal terror. Gill localises both halves, the sword outside being the besieging army that destroyed all who tried to come or go, and the sword within the weapons of the factions who destroyed multitudes among themselves.

Then the sentence turns, and the turn is what interests them. Henry marks it as surprising intimations of mercy after so many terrible threatenings, mercy wholly undeserved, which rejoices against judgment and shows that God has no pleasure in the death of sinners; and he states the ground, that in jealousy for his own honour God will not make a full end. Keil says the same more plainly, that the people had deserved to be utterly destroyed and were spared for another reason than their own. Calvin describes the form the statement takes: God again represents himself under the character of a man, as though meditating opposite determinations and restraining his own vehemence at the obstacles he meets; what it comes to is that he suspended the final judgment for no other reason than regard to his own glory, which would otherwise have been exposed to the taunts of the nations. Gill presses the opening verb, which he would render that God could have said or might have said, since it was in his power and justice to do what follows.

Whose anger is feared is disputed. Clarke reports that some would refer the word not to the enemy at all but to God, and gives their rendering, that indignation for the adversary deters him lest the enemies be alienated and say that the strength of their own hands and not the Lord's had done this; his own point is that unless the punishment had been of a kind that proved whose hand it was, the heathen would have drawn the wrong conclusion. Wesley keeps the common reading and fills it out as the enemy's rage and furious reproaches against God's name, as though he were cruel to his people or unable to deliver them, adding that the fear of it is ascribed to God after the manner of men. Ellicott offers alternatives for the following verb, either that they should misunderstand the matter or that they should take note of it as a strange thing. Gill alone identifies the enemy otherwise, as the adversary of mankind and of God himself, full of wrath and blasphemy, who stirs up the like in the hearts of men.
28:
Who is described here governs the whole passage, and it is not settled. Gill holds that the prophecy against the one people has been discharged and that another is now in view, namely their enemies, and he carries that through the rest of the passage. Wesley agrees at the opening, calling the enemies a foolish people who therefore judge falsely of things. Calvin reads it the other way, assigning the cause why the memory of the people had almost been blotted out, that their folly was incurable, the charge being not merely that their conduct was rash for want of discretion but that they could by no means be brought to their senses. Ellicott renders the phrase literally as perishing in counsels, or perhaps as spoiling the plans of the Lord, and sets beside it the resolve of men who devised devices against a prophet in the confidence that counsel would never fail from the wise.

The wish that follows is guarded by Gill against a use he will not allow. These are not the words of God, he says, and so give no instance of an unsuccessful wish in him, nor any argument that a man may make himself wise if he will; they are the words of Moses under a spirit of prophecy. On what is to be considered the readings part. Clarke takes the phrase of their latter times and makes it the days of the Messiah who was to spring from them, so that a people receiving the promised Saviour would act as men under infinite obligations. Ellicott renders it as discernment about their hereafter, what their destiny was and what they will miss if they fail to fulfil it. Wesley makes it plainer and grimmer, what their end will be, and that though God spare them long, judgment will certainly overtake them at last.

The arithmetic of the rout is taken by all as proof. Calvin says the token is chosen as peculiarly striking: while God was on their side they routed mighty armies without numbers of their own, and now, being many, are conquered by a few, which shows plainly that his help is withdrawn. Keil states the same conditionally, that a wise Israel could easily have conquered all its foes in the power of its God, and was given up only because it had forsaken its rock. Ellicott notes that the verb rendered sold is here used of the Lord for the first time, and Wesley fills out both verbs, sold for bondslaves and shut up as in the net their enemies had laid.

On the comparison of the two rocks the sense of one clause divides them. Clarke takes the enemies as witnesses who concede the point, since they often acknowledged the irresistible power of the God who fought for Israel, and adds a parallel from a Latin poet; Wesley says dear-bought experience forced them to own that this God was stronger than they and their gods together. Ellicott proposes another construction, on a rabbinic authority, in which the clause means that our enemies are lords over us, the verse standing as a parenthesis and the argument running that no cause can be found for the defeat except the Lord's displeasure. On the vine that follows, Ellicott states expressly that it is Israel's and not the enemies', and Clarke and Wesley read it the same way, Clarke taking the grapes for their actions and the clusters for their united as well as their several deeds. Calvin denies that the words refer, as some make them, to the punishment the people deserved, and takes them for an invective against their morals, calling them an offshoot of that older vine because they resemble those nations as nearly as if sprung from them. Gill keeps his other reading and applies the vine to corrupt professors within the empire that destroyed the city.
34:
What is laid up in store is disputed. Calvin reports the view that it is the punishments, as though various kinds of them were kept by God to be produced at will, and prefers the crimes, since the ungodly promise themselves impunity whenever God stays his severity and treat his forbearance as connivance. Wesley reads it the same way, the long-suffering making them think their sins forgotten while they are remembered punctually and sealed up as in a bag; Gill takes it likewise of practices laid up in the divine memory. Ellicott is less sure: the pronoun is generally referred to what follows, though it may point back to the vine that yielded wild grapes. Clarke supplies the legal figure behind the sealing, that deeds binding men to fulfil conditions at a stated time were sealed and laid up in safety, so that justice stands pledged to avenge the broken covenant while the time and manner remain known only to God.

On the vengeance itself Gill draws a fence. It belongs to a divine person only, not to any heathen deity of that name, nor to Satan and his angels, nor to private men, whatever be said of magistrates in office; and the ancient versions, he notes, render the clause as a promise to repay. Ellicott points out that the sentence is quoted in two epistles, once with the opening of the next verse, and corrects the following clause to read of the time when their foot shall slide. Wesley presses both halves, that those who think they stand unmoveable shall fall, that the due time is not so soon as some expect but when the measure of their sins is full, and that Scripture often calls near what is many hundred years off, distance in our measures of time being nothing in God's. Clarke reports a commentator who refers the verse not to Israel but to the Canaanites.

Whether the next verse threatens or consoles is the sharpest division here. Ellicott, following the use made of it in an epistle, says that to judge here means to punish, not to defend. Wesley reads it the opposite way, that the discourse now turns into a more comfortable strain and that to judge his people is to plead their cause and deliver them after they have been sorely chastised. Calvin states both and resolves them by a distinction: some connect the sentence with what precedes and the apostle seems to support them, using it to prove how fearful a thing it is to fall into the hands of the living God, but there is no reason why an apostle should not accommodate to another purpose what was set down for the consolation of the godly. Clarke holds both together, that God has right to punish them as their Sovereign and yet will change his conduct towards them when their power is wholly gone and not one strong place is left untaken. Ellicott adds a rendering by which God will be comforted over his servants, and Keil takes the turn as the moment when the people are convinced of the worthlessness of idols.

Who asks after the gods is the last question. Gill denies that the Lord is upbraiding Israel and, on the authority of the Targums, puts the taunt in the enemy's mouth, adding that the words may be rendered impersonally and in the singular. Calvin sets out the same two options, that Moses is either reporting the boastings of enemies over an afflicted Church or recording a pious exultation of the faithful over her deliverance, and argues against the first from the plural form of the word for gods. Clarke takes a third course, making it God who expostulates in order to awaken them to their ingratitude, and suggesting that this may look forward to the preaching of the Gospel in the latter days.
39:
Who is speaking at the turn depends on how the preceding verses were assigned. Calvin notes that those who gave them to the unbelievers must now bring God in abruptly, asserting his glory in rebuke of their blasphemies, whereas he takes the words as a confirmation of the holy boasting just put into the mouths of the faithful. Henry treats the whole as the conclusion of the song and hears in it a demand for the glory of self-existence, the name by which the speaker had first been made to know God. Ellicott observes that many passages in one prophet run close to this without exactly reproducing it, and that the following clause was taken up afterwards in a woman's song of thanksgiving. Clarke states the practical point, that God alone can save and destroy while the idols can neither hurt nor help, and adds that the mercy is as great as the justice, since he is as ready to save the penitent as he was to punish the rebellious. Gill directs the words to a people in their low estate and to the enemies who insult them; Wesley reduces them to a lesson learned by sad experience, what vain and impotent things idols are.

The lifted hand is taken by all as an oath, and its background is supplied by two. Gill notes that this is the gesture used in swearing and is ascribed to a divine person, and reports that although the same action is sometimes used merely to excite the attention of hearers, here it means an oath, the Targums paraphrasing it so. Wesley reduces it to two clauses, that God solemnly swears and that it is as sure as he lives. Calvin reports a rendering that would make it when I shall have lifted up my hand and join it to the verse before, but does not doubt that a new sentence begins here, framed to give greater force to what follows. Keil marks the same point as the close of the ode, and calls its closing promise one full of comfort for all the servants of the Lord.

The conditional clause that follows is construed three ways. Gill takes it as the suppressed half of an oath, as if to say that it will be done as surely as God lives, and if not, then let such and such follow, the consequence being left for the hearer to conclude. Calvin will not leave the matter in suspense and resolves the particle into an adverb of time, so that as soon as God takes up arms the destruction of his enemies is certain; he adds that God wants no weapons. Wesley reads it plainly as a condition of beginning, and glosses the second noun as the instruments of judgment, a metaphor from warriors taking their weapons in hand. Gill describes the sword itself, drawn and polished and whetted so that when brandished it glitters like lightning.

The last verse of the threat is textually the hardest, and Clarke says so. The word rendered revenges he holds never to bear that sense, which has made the place perplexed and obscure, and he sets out another scholar's version ending instead with the hairy head of the enemy. Ellicott keeps the received sense and renders from the blood of the slain and of the captivity, from the beginning of revenges upon the enemy, adding that judgment must begin at the house of God as in a prophet's vision where it began at the sanctuary. Calvin describes what is intended without settling the words, a horrible massacre with no end to the vengeance until the earth is full of blood and corpses. Wesley distinguishes the captives as sorely wounded though not utterly killed, and takes the last clause to mean that once the vengeance begins it will make a full end.
44:
How the song was delivered is reconstructed the same way by two. Henry supposes that Moses spoke it to as many as could hear him while Joshua at the same time delivered it in another assembly to as many as his own voice would reach, and draws the point from the arrangement: coming from the mouth of both governors, the one laying down the office and the other taking it up, the people could see that the two were of one mind. Wesley gives the same reconstruction and adds that Joshua as well as Moses would thus be a witness against them if ever they forsook God. Keil states only that the two spoke it together and that the closing exhortation impressed the importance of the commandments once more, and he observes that this account comes from the hand that supplied the appendix to the books of Moses. Gill and Clarke both suppose that Moses came from the tabernacle, Gill on the authority of a Targum which calls it the house of instruction and Clarke because the ode had been given him there.

Ellicott alone stops at the name. Why should Joshua be called Hoshea in this place, when the name had apparently been changed at the time he went with the eleven others to search out the land? He answers that now, when the man is about to lead the people to the conquest, the reader is reminded once more of the change and of what it meant, that the salvation of the Lord was to be shown forth through him.

Calvin draws a different lesson from the mere fact of the repetition. That Moses records having spoken the song again before the people shows how far he was from all ambition, since at the very close of his life he did not fear to irritate every mind against him and to make the memory of his own name hateful; and his authority is confirmed from the other side too, by the silence and submissiveness of the hearers, who let themselves be dealt with so severely without protest.

The closing charge is where Clarke makes his largest claim. He takes it as another proof that all these awful denunciations of divine wrath, delivered though they are in an absolute form, were only declaratory of what God would do if the people rebelled; and on the promise attached he says that instead of being cut off as the song threatens they would be preserved and made prosperous in the land. Ellicott corrects the second clause to read that they may command their children, and observes that for a long time to come the knowledge of the law must have depended very largely on personal instruction; he cites a rabbinic parallel for the charge to set the heart on all the words. On the last verse he renders the opening as meaning that the thing is not too light for them and not unworthy of their attention, and marks it as the last time in the book that the people are assured that the very end of their existence in the land was the keeping of this law as the law of the land. Gill says the same more briefly, that it was no light or trifling matter but one of great consequence, obedience being attended with rewards and disobedience with punishment.
48:
Calvin denies that these verses stand in their proper order. It is certain, he argues, that Moses was warned of his approaching death before the song was composed, and a second passage confirms it, since the place where he was to die had been pointed out to him before Joshua was substituted for him; and he adds that an inverted order of narration is by no means unusual. The others take the day at face value. Gill fixes it as the day on which the reading of the law and the song was finished, gives the month and day, reports a Targum which makes it the day of his death, and notes another calendar that places it later in the same month. Ellicott says only that it was the day on which the song was spoken in the ears of all Israel.

What the timing shows about the man is drawn out by two. Wesley asks why, having finished his work, he should wish to live a day longer, and observes that though he had formerly prayed to go over Jordan he is now entirely satisfied and says no more of the matter. Henry asks the same question in the same words and then turns to the reminder of the old sin for which he was kept out of the land, drawing the lesson that it is good for the best of men to die repenting the infirmities they are conscious of, while adding that those who have a believing prospect may die with comfort and ease whenever God calls, notwithstanding the sins they remember against themselves.

The mountain is identified by degrees. Clarke gives the meaning of the range as the mount of the passages, that is, of the people when they entered the promised land. Wesley and Gill add that the peak named is a ridge or summit of that range. Ellicott supplies the history of the command: it had been given once before and was answered then by the prayer for a successor, which was granted, so that everything narrated between that passage and this may be counted preliminary to the departure; and he points out that the particular peak on which the death was to happen had not been named until now. Keil states the charge itself, to go up, to see the land given for a possession, and to die there and be gathered to his people as his brother had been on another mountain.

That word about the brother is the hinge of Clarke's last argument. Some have supposed that Moses was translated rather than that he died; but if so, he answers, then Aaron was translated too, since what is said of the death of the one is said of the death of the other. Gill takes the command plainly, that immediately after the view of the land he was to expect death, prepare for it, and submit to it willingly. On the reason given for the sentence Gill names two faults, an unbelief that doubted whether God would give water to so rebellious a people, and a giving way to passion and wrathful words. Wesley marks the timing of the reminder, that God recalls a sin committed long before, and repeats that it is good for the holiest of men to die repenting even of their early faults. Calvin weighs what the sentence cost: death in itself would not have been so bitter, but the cause alleged wounded the holy man grievously, since he saw himself shut out by God's just vengeance from the common inheritance on account of his own guilt, and to the pious that is more afflictive than many deaths.
